description: Learn the industry-standard framework for building fast, concurrent, and robust web crawlers.

slides.title: What is Scrapy?
slides.content:
# The Heavy Lifter 🏗️

`requests` + `BeautifulSoup` is great for small scripts. But what if you want to scrape 10,000 pages?

If you use `requests` in a `for` loop, it downloads one page at a time (synchronously). It will take hours.

**Scrapy** is an open-source web-crawling framework written in Python. It is **Asynchronous** (built on Twisted), meaning it can download dozens of pages concurrently, making it blisteringly fast!

slides.title: Creating a Scrapy Project
slides.content:
# Project Architecture 📁

Scrapy isn't just a library; it's a framework that generates a whole project structure for you.

## Setup
```bash
pip install scrapy
scrapy startproject my_scraper
```

This creates a directory with this structure:
```text
my_scraper/
    scrapy.cfg            # deploy configuration file
    my_scraper/           # project's Python module
        __init__.py
        items.py          # project items definition file
        middlewares.py    # project middlewares file
        pipelines.py      # project pipelines file
        settings.py       # project settings file
        spiders/          # directory where you put your Spiders
```

slides.title: The Spider
CSS and XPath in Scrapy
slides.content:
# Built-in Selectors 🎯

Notice in the previous slide, we didn't import BeautifulSoup! Scrapy comes with its own extremely fast selector engine based on `lxml`.

Every `response` object has `.css()` and `.xpath()` methods built right in!

```python_not
# CSS Selector
title = response.css('title::text').get()

# XPath Equivalent
title = response.xpath('//title/text()').get()

# Getting multiple elements
all_links = response.css('a::attr(href)').getall()
```

> 💡 **Tip:** `::text` and `::attr(name)` are special pseudo-selectors added by Scrapy to easily extract text and attributes using CSS syntax!

slides.title: Yielding Data
slides.content:
# The Power of Yield 🚂

In Scrapy `parse` methods, you rarely use `return`. Instead, you use the `yield` keyword.

When you `yield` a **Dictionary** (or an `Item`), Scrapy knows this is extracted data, and passes it to the Item Pipelines.

When you `yield` a **Request** (e.g., `yield scrapy.Request(url)`), Scrapy adds that URL to its queue to be downloaded asynchronously!

slides.title: Scrapy Items
slides.content:
# Structured Data (Items) 📦

While yielding dictionaries works, for large projects, it's better to define a strict structure for your scraped data. 

In `items.py`, you define `Item` classes:

```python_not
import scrapy

class ProductItem(scrapy.Item):
    name = scrapy.Field()
    price = scrapy.Field()
    stock = scrapy.Field()
```

Now, in your spider, you use it like a dict:
```python_not
item = ProductItem()
item['name'] = response.css('h1::text').get()
# Scrapy will throw an error if you try to assign item['fake_field']!
yield item
```

slides.title: Item Pipelines
slides.content:
# Data Assembly Line 🏭

Once a Spider yields an Item, it goes to the **Item Pipeline**. 
Pipelines are Python classes used to cleanse, validate, or store the scraped data.

Example `pipelines.py`:
```python_not
import sqlite3

class DatabasePipeline:
    def open_spider(self, spider):
        self.conn = sqlite3.connect('scraped_data.db')
        self.cursor = self.conn.cursor()
        self.cursor.execute('CREATE TABLE products (name TEXT, price REAL)')

    def process_item(self, item, spider):
        # Clean price string '$19.99' -> 19.99
        clean_price = float(item['price'].replace('$', ''))
        
        # Save to database
        self.cursor.execute('INSERT INTO products VALUES (?, ?)', (item['name'], clean_price))
        self.conn.commit()
        return item

    def close_spider(self, spider):
        self.conn.close()
```

slides.title: Activating Pipelines
slides.content:
# Settings Configuration ⚙️

Pipelines don't run automatically! You must enable them in `settings.py`.

```python_not
# settings.py
ITEM_PIPELINES = {
   'my_scraper.pipelines.DatabasePipeline': 300,
}
```

The integer `300` defines the execution order. If you have multiple pipelines (e.g., CleanDataPipeline, ValidatePipeline, DatabasePipeline), they execute from lowest to highest number.

slides.title: The CrawlSpider
slides.content:
# Automated Crawling 🕸️

Writing `response.follow()` for pagination is easy, but what if you want to scrape an entire e-commerce site with thousands of categories and product links?

Scrapy provides the `CrawlSpider`, which uses **Rules** to automatically follow links!

```python_not
from scrapy.spiders import CrawlSpider, Rule
from scrapy.linkextractors import LinkExtractor

class StoreSpider(CrawlSpider):
    name = "store"
    start_urls = ['http://store.example.com']

    rules = (
        # Follow category links automatically (don't parse them)
        Rule(LinkExtractor(allow=r'/category/')), 
        
        # Follow product links AND call parse_item to scrape data
        Rule(LinkExtractor(allow=r'/product/'), callback='parse_item'),
    )

    def parse_item(self, response):
        # Scrape the product page
        pass
```

slides.title: LinkExtractors
slides.content:
# Fine-Tuning Link Extraction 🔗

`LinkExtractor` objects are incredibly powerful. They use regular expressions and CSS/XPath selectors to find specific links to follow.

```python_not
LinkExtractor(
    allow=r'/item/\d+',          # Only follow links matching this regex
    deny=r'/cart',               # NEVER follow these links
    restrict_css='.pagination',  # Only look for links inside pagination divs!
    tags=('a', 'area')           # Look for hrefs in these tags
)
```
This allows you to map out exactly how the spider traverses a massive website!

slides.title: Middlewares
slides.content:
# Scrapy Middlewares 🛡️

Middlewares sit between the Spider and the Internet. They intercept Requests going out, and Responses coming in.

## Downloader Middleware Uses:
- Rotating Proxies (changing IP addresses so you don't get banned)
- Rotating User-Agents
- Adding Custom Headers
- Handling Captchas automatically

```python_not
class RotateAgentMiddleware:
    def process_request(self, request, spider):
        request.headers['User-Agent'] = get_random_agent()
        return None
```

slides.title: FormRequest
Feed Exports
slides.content:
# Exporting Data Automatically 💾

You don't *have* to write a Pipeline to save data to a CSV or JSON file.
Scrapy has built-in "Feed Exports".

You can trigger this right from the command line!

```bash
# Scrape and save to JSON
scrapy crawl quotes -o quotes.json

# Scrape and save to CSV
scrapy crawl quotes -o quotes.csv

# Scrape and save to XML
scrapy crawl quotes -o quotes.xml
```

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Summary 🎉

You are now equipped to build industrial-grade web crawlers!

## Key Takeaways
- ✅ **Asynchronous Power:** Scrapy downloads pages concurrently, making it extremely fast.
- ✅ **Spiders:** Define the starting URLs and parsing logic.
- ✅ **Items:** Define the strict data structure of the scraped payload.
- ✅ **Pipelines:** Process, clean, and store the Items yielded by the spider.
- ✅ **CrawlSpider & Rules:** Automate the discovery and following of links without writing complex pagination logic manually.
- ✅ **Middlewares:** Intercept requests to rotate proxies and user-agents to avoid IP bans.
- ✅ **Feed Exports:** Save data to CSV/JSON with a simple `-o filename` command line flag.
